# Mahāsīlavajātaka (Ja 51)
**ID:** Ja 51
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahāsīlavajātaka* (Ja 51) is a narrative in the Jātaka collection centering on the perfection of moral conduct, non-violence, and undaunted determination [SuttaCentral; Sarkisyanz 1965]. The frame story (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha addresses a monk who had abandoned energetic effort (*ossatthaviriya*). To encourage him, the Buddha recounts how wise beings of the past maintained their resolution even after losing their sovereignty, prompting the canonical verse beginning *Āsimsetheva puriso* ("A person should indeed hope") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Following the discourse, the discouraged monk attains arahantship [Fausböll 1877].
In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta is born as Mahāsīlava, the righteous and compassionate king of Benares, who establishes extensive almshalls and governs with loving-kindness [Thomas 1950; Sharf]. When a corrupt minister is expelled for misconduct in the royal harem, the traitor incites the king of Kośala to invade Benares [Law 1926; Cowell 1897; Sharf]. Refusing to allow any bloodshed in self-defense, King Mahāsīlava forbids resistance, declaring that none should suffer on his account [Deegalle 2006; Sarkisyanz 1965]. The invader captures the king and his ministers and buries them alive up to their necks in a charnel pit [Law 1926; Sharf]. King Mahāsīlava extricates himself and frees his men; he then adjudicates a dispute between two demons (*yakkhas*) squabbling over a corpse by cleaving the body in half with a sword [Law 1926; Sharf]. Grateful for his fair division, the demons miraculously assist him in confronting the usurper in his bedchamber, moving the aggressor through his moral power and regaining his kingdom [Law 1926; Sarkisyanz 1965; Sharf]. In the resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the treacherous minister was Devadatta, the loyal ministers were the Buddha's assembly, and King Mahāsīlava was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877].
SuttaCentral notes passage-level parallels to the *Sarabhamigajātaka* (Ja 483) and the *Mahājanakajātaka* (Ja 539), both of which emphasize steadfast resolution in adversity [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects no significant Pali-internal or cross-language matches above the indexing threshold [DharmaNexus]. Modern scholars have examined the tale both for its folklore motifs—such as the bickering-demon sequence in charnel grounds—and as a prominent text in Buddhist political ethics and pacifism [Deegalle 2006; Sarkisyanz 1965; Sharf].
